summary.value: This paper proposes a unified Bayesian framework for understanding how in-context learning (ICL) and activation steering control large language model behavior. The authors argue that both methods operate by updating an LLM's beliefs over latent concepts: ICL accumulates evidence through likelihood functions while activation steering modifies concept priors. They derive a predictive model that captures sigmoidal ICL curves, steering-induced curve shifts, and additive interaction effects. Experiments across three LLMs on five persona-manipulation tasks show the model achieves high predictive accuracy.

strengths.value: The theoretical unification of ICL and activation steering through Bayesian belief updating is conceptually elegant.

weaknesses.value:
Circular dependency in steering vector construction: 

The paper claims that activation steering modifies priors p(c) independently of context (Section 3.2). However, steering vectors are constructed using the CAA method (Eq. 2), which requires processing demonstrations Dc and Dc' through the model—the same demonstrations that could be used directly for ICL.
This creates a conceptual problem: if steering vectors are derived from demonstrations, then the "context-independent prior modification" actually depends on contextual information. The distinction between "steering modifies priors" versus "ICL accumulates evidence" may simply be two different ways of using the same information from demonstrations, rather than genuinely independent mechanisms.
The paper should clarify whether steering can be constructed without demonstrations, or if the theoretical framework is primarily describing how demonstration-derived information can be "pre-compiled" into steering vectors for later application.

questions.value: Statistical testing only contains correlations, lacking confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparisons to simpler baseline models.

summary.value: This paper worked on controlling LLM inference time behaviour by proposing a unified Bayesian framework with belief updating. While the merits of the paper (e.g.,  conceptually elegant, well-written) appreciated by reviewers, there are several key weaknesses that concern the reviewers (and myself). Although the authors partially addressed some of these concerns during the rebuttal, major weaknesses remain.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their comments, and for describing our theory as “conceptually elegant”. While our theoretical framing is an important part of this work, we would also like to highlight that we believe our empirical findings are also essential to its novelty and overall contribution. 

----

> **Circular dependency in steering vector construction...**

We agree that there is a compelling relationship between ICL and activation steering in their connection with demonstrations $D_c$ and $D_{c’}$. However, we argue that this relationship is not circular. In any case where we have steering vectors which influence the same concept as a set of ICL examples, we can think of this as “compiling” information about that concept into steering vectors, regardless of whether demonstrations are used to construct steering vectors. Our model formalizes this equivalence as altering belief in latent concepts, and this theory applies equally regardless of how steering vectors are constructed.

For the reviewer’s question of “whether steering can be constructed without demonstrations”, we think this is an interesting question but goes far beyond the goals of our work. While steering vectors can be constructed without labelled demonstrations, it is unclear how we could interpret whether a steering vector matches a particular concept, which is critical for our experiments. E.g. if we used SAEs to produce steering vectors for latent features without explicit demonstrations, if we then tried to identify which features align with a particular concept (e.g. a psychopathic persona) by identifying and classifying examples which maximally activate a feature, it is unclear why this would be any different from using demonstrations to train the vector. Further, one might argue that SAEs are learning from unlabelled demonstrations of latent concepts in the original training data.

----

**Questions**

> **Statistical testing only contains correlations, lacking confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparisons to simpler baseline models.**

Thank you for the suggestion! Our correlation analyses in Sec. 3 and in Fig. 7 have been updated with p-values for correlations, which are all $p<.001$. We do not include comparison to alternate baseline models since it is unclear to us what baseline model would be able to predict $N*$ out-of-sample. For example, if we included an alternative model which ablates magnitude, the predictions for $N*$ would all be the same value regardless of magnitude (i.e. low correlation with the true $N$ values), and the comparison to our full model would seem trivial.

----
----

> **Out of curiosity – it seems that one interesting thing here is that the ICL examples come from some dataset of examples, and vary in number, while the CAA vectors are constructed from some other (potentially overlapping) dataset, and are fixed. Do you think there is a correspondence between a particular set of in-context examples, and some steering vector? I.e. is there a steering vector which affects the model's beliefs in a way that is precisely equivalent to including those examples in context?**

Great question! We wondered about this ourselves, and added an experiment to Appendix G which tests whether steering vectors constructed from increasing numbers of ICL examples are similar to steering vectors constructed from individual shots. Surprisingly, we find that steering vectors constructed from multiple shots have a weaker effect than steering vectors constructed from “0-shot” examples, although this steering effect increases with larger number of shots. Another surprising finding of this experiment is that the multiple-shot steering vectors increasingly diverge from the steering vectors used in our main experiment, instead converging towards the 128-shot steering vector. While this experiment is preliminary and demands further work in order to draw a conclusive answer to your question, these findings might suggest that the answer is no, unless steering vectors are constructed in a different way than what we have considered here.

**Summary**: We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and suggestions that have helped us improve our work! We hope our responses helped address their concerns and, if so, we hope that they will consider raising their score and championing our paper during the discussion period.

We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments and suggestions. We appreciate that they found our method to be “interesting”, and appreciated how our results and the predictive accuracy of our model support our theory. Below, we provide more detailed responses to comments raised by the reviewer. 

----

> **The model assumes linear representation of belief and separable concept directions, which may not hold for complex or abstract concepts.**

Indeed, we agree that the Linear Representation Hypothesis makes a strong assumption about linearity and independence of concept directions! For complex or abstract concepts, e.g., concepts with hierarchical or other structured relationships, we expect the geometry to be more complex. One example of this is [1], where the authors found that complex graphical relationships between in-context concepts are reflected in analogous relationships across hidden representations.
We are enthusiastic about extending our belief dynamics model by relaxing these assumptions in future work, which we are actively pursuing. Concretely, this involves modifying our Equation 8 (where  $\log o(c | x) \propto a \cdot m$) so that the log posterior odds are updated linearly according to a function $f$, i.e. $\log o(c | x) \propto f(a, m)$. This function relates to a projection operator for more complex geometries than simple lines. We are excited about this follow up because it can enable us to do activation steering with complex domains such as [1], which (by authors’ own admission in the paper) was difficult.

[1] Park, C. F., Lee, A., Lubana, E. S., Yang, Y., Okawa, M., Nishi, K., ... & Tanaka, H. ICLR: In-Context Learning of Representations. In The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations.

----

> **The experiments focus on binary, persona-style datasets. Generalization to open-ended or multi-concept tasks remains uncertain.**

Fair point! To demonstrate our results generalize to more complex settings, we have added an additional experiment to Appendix F which applies the same Bayesian model to such a setting. In particular, we consider the task of flipped-label sentiment analysis, where there are three possible labels (negative, neutral, positive) and the model learns, through ICL and steering, a new concept which rotates the ordering of these sentiment labels (label negative → neutral, neutral → positive, positive → negative). We find similar results in this domain as in our main persona experiments: our Bayesian model is equally predictive of changes to LLM behavior. The primary difference we observe is that ICL requires more samples to converge and we only observe ceiling performance with the combination of high steering magnitudes and large numbers of ICL samples. As mentioned in our response to your previous question, we are also excited to extend our model and show corresponding results with tasks where the concept space is more complex and structured.

----

> **While the Bayesian model predicts empirical data well, it is unclear how it performs out-of-domain or on unseen LLM architectures.**

Thank you for the comment. We believe there is a possible misunderstanding here. Specifically, we emphasize that our Bayesian model (Eq. 8) includes free parameters $a, b, \gamma, \alpha$, which are fit separately to LLM behavioral data across each analyzed task. Correspondingly, *these parameters are expected to take different values on different datasets and different LLMs*, e.g. $b$ which measures the prior odds of a given concept has to depend on the specific concept being analyzed. We do also emphasize that what we expect is for our functional, i.e., the Bayesian model derived in the paper, to hold in cases with easily measurable concepts, and with LLMs where belief is represented linearly in at least one layer.

----

**Questions**

> **Are the observed phase boundaries consistent across different LLM sizes (e.g., 70B+ models), or do scaling laws alter belief dynamics?**

Good question! We have now added results with larger LLMs to Appendix D. We find that, as with smaller LLMs, in-context learning and steering jointly affect behavior, and that we are able to predict behavior across varying context lengths and steering magnitudes with a high correlation (cross-validated out-of-sample r=0.98). In contrast with smaller models, ICL occurs substantially faster, and the models begin to match the persona with merely a few examples, whereas for smaller models in many cases more examples are required.

----

**(Continued below...)**

Thank you for the feedback! We are glad that the Reviewer appreciates our mathematical derivation of the relationship between representation change and concept probability, as well as our “well-designed experiments” which “support the predictions from the mathematical formulations”. Below, we respond to specific comments raised by the reviewer.

----

> **(1) The paper assumes in L294: …**

This was an error in our previous draft, we have removed this sentence and amended the surrounding text appropriately. Thanks for the pointer!

----

> **(2) Equation (6) is not clear to me. Could the author give a step-by-step derivation?**

We apologize for the confusion. We have now added a new section in the appendix (see A.2), which provides a step-by-step derivation of Equation 6.

----

> **(3) The term "concept-consistent label" is used but not defined. What is the meaning of "concept-consistent label"? what does  mean?**

We use the term “concept-consistent label” $y_i^{(c)}$ to refer to outputs (labels) that align with a concept $c$ instead of some other concept $c’$. In our tasks, outputs have a one-to-one mapping with the concept value, and hence we need only focus our analysis on such labels that are consistent with the concept. Thanks for the question—we have updated the text to clarify this point!

----

> **(4) The considered datasets are "we used a selection of datasets that represent relatively low-probability concepts in LLMs, yet consist of behaviors that a sufficiently capable LLM would be able to follow accurately." While this is a suitable choice for experiments, it also limits the dataset's diversity. In other words, we do not know whether the "sigmoid" phenomenon happens for a high-probability concept.**

Fair point! We have now added new experimental results in Appendix E where results on higher-probability “persona” concepts—including, “openness”, “interest in science”, “interest in music”, and “desire to create allies”—are reported. Since the LLM’s belief in these concepts is much higher a priori, we do not observe a full sigmoidal trend, instead we observe only the end of the sigmoid where behavior rapidly plateaus with more examples. Here we also find that our belief dynamics model is effective at predicting LLM behavior.

We have also added new experimental results in Appendix F for a more complicated domain: flipped-label sentiment analysis. In this task, where a model is expected to classify inputs by sentiment (positive, neutral, negative), we intentionally permute the labels such that the pretraining prior of “positive sentiment” queries mapping to the label “positive” will not work anymore. In this setting, we find similar belief dynamics as in our main experiments and our Bayesian model is highly predictive of LLM behavior (although we note that the LLM requires many more ICL samples to converge in this task).

Thank you for the suggestions!

----

**Questions**

> **(1) In visualizations of Figures 3 and 4, some curves look like a sigmoid, and some are not (such as Figure 4, bottom right). How do we convince ourselves that the curve is sigmoid?**

We note that results such as Fig 4 (bottom right) can be understood as a subset of a sigmoid curve. When we expand the x-axis to show the full span of magnitudes tested (see Appendix C), the sigmoid curve becomes more apparent, along with the subsequent degradation of model behavior which occurs with high-magnitude activation steering. We have updated the text in Section 4.1 to clarify this point.

**Summary**: We thank the reviewer for their detailed feedback which has motivated us to include further experiments, and which have helped us improve the quality and presentation of our work! We hope that our responses have helped resolve their concerns, and if so, that they will consider raising their score.

We are grateful to the reviewer for their positive feedback and thoughtful comments. We are glad they found our paper “conceptually elegant, clearly written, and well-executed”, and especially that though our work has “potential to have a strong impact, both on the ICLR community and at large” by making progress on “one of the most important topics in LLM research today”. Below, we respond to specific comments raised by the reviewer. 

----

> **I think the paper would be strengthened by showing that the predictive model still works well in additional settings beyond the 5 shown. At the moment, I am unsure how general the method is along the "task" axis. If I recall correctly, there are 30-50 persona evals in Perez et al. Would we expect the results to hold up for all of them?**

Thank you for the helpful suggestion! We have extended our results to include an additional set of tasks from the persona evals of Perez et al. in Appendix E. This set includes both low and high prior personas. In these experiments, we find similar belief dynamics as in our persona experiments which can be well-explained by our Bayesian model; however, the effects are less visible in high-prior concepts since model behavior is relatively close to ceiling even before steering or ICL. 

Further, we have also extended our results to the flipped-label sentiment analysis of [1] in Appendix F, which is a more complex three-label task (not included in Perez et al.) where the LLM must learn a rotated mapping of labels [negative, neutral, positive]. In these cases, we also observe similar belief dynamics as in our main persona experiments which our Bayesian model can predict. The main deviation we notice is that ICL requires more samples to converge for this task, and we hence only observe ceiling performance with the combination of high steering magnitudes and large numbers of ICL samples.

[1] Agarwal, R., Singh, A., Zhang, L., Bohnet, B., Rosias, L., Chan, S., ... & Larochelle, H. (2024). Many-shot in-context learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 37, 76930-76966.

----

> **Relatedly, I am curious if the authors have any thoughts or experimental evidence on whether we expect the broad behaviors (but not the theory) to generalize to more complex settings beyond concept learning. In particular, many recent works have studied how language models learn in-context in simple decision-making settings such as bandit tasks [1,2,3,4], where the latter of those finds that steering vectors can modulate an agent's belief state about what action is best to take. Could the authors share any thoughts on how we could understand steering vs. ICL for decision-making?**

This is an exciting direction to consider, given that in other domains we might not expect the same power-law ICL scaling as we observe in our experiments. Our belief dynamics model could be altered to use alternate likelihood functions which better match particular tasks, for example multi-armed bandits, or other cases such as [1, 2] which frame ICL as Bayesian belief updating, but empirically observe different kinds of ICL dynamics with LLMs.

One obstacle to testing our work in such settings is limitations of our method of CAA activation steering, which requires contrastive datasets corresponding to two concepts (e.g. a particular persona and its inverse). The work you have cited here, Rahn et al. (2024), is a compelling approach for steering in decision making settings, but one which requires more thought to account for the additional assumptions introduced by their method of steering vector construction. Another obstacle is that decision making settings involve sampling rollouts where the LLM takes actions and receives feedback in-context, which would complicate our analysis since behavior is not only a function of input data (i.e. ICL examples) but also a function of output actions the LLM takes at each step. This is another direction we are especially interested in exploring in future work, to account for settings where autoregressive text generation, such as actions in a decision-making setting, interacts with ICL.

[1] Schubert, J. A., Jagadish, A. K., Binz, M., & Schulz, E. (2024). In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters.

[2] Bigelow, E. J., Lubana, E. S., Dick, R. P., Tanaka, H., & Ullman, T. D. (2023). In-context learning dynamics with random binary sequences.

----

**(Continued below...)**

summary.value: This paper studies the interaction between modulating an LLM's behavior through in-context learning and activation steering on multiple-choice-based persona evals. Importantly, the authors develop a Bayesian theory of the effects of these two interventions, with the prediction being that steering modulates the prior odds of a particular concept, and ICL leads to the accumulation of evidence for a particular concept. The paper finds that the resulting model is highly predictive of the behavior we observe in practice.

strengths.value: The paper is conceptually elegant, clearly written, and well-executed. Specifically, the central idea that steering modulates priors and ICL accumulates evidence is quite natural (perhaps in hindsight!), and the accompanying theory appears to be sound given the assumptions it makes. The quality of the writing and presentation is high – I found the diagrams to clearly communicate the structure and goals of the method, and the numerical figures support the claims being made. While the current execution has some limitations, I think this work has the potential to have a strong impact, both on the ICLR community and at large, as understanding the relationships between the different test-time interventions we can make on LLMs is arguably one of the most important topics in LLM research today.

- I think the paper would be strengthened by showing that the predictive model still works well in additional settings beyond the 5 shown. At the moment, I am unsure how general the method is along the "task" axis. If I recall correctly, there are 30-50 persona evals in Perez et al. Would we expect the results to hold up for all of them?

In particular, many recent works have studied how language models learn in-context in simple decision-making settings such as bandit tasks [1,2,3,4], where the latter of those finds that steering vectors can modulate an agent's belief state about what action is best to take. Could the authors share any thoughts on how we could understand steering vs. ICL for decision-making?

[3] Nie, Allen, et al. "Evolve: Evaluating and optimizing llms for exploration." arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.06238 (2024). 
[4] Rahn, Nate, Pierluca D'Oro, and Marc G. Bellemare. "Controlling Large Language Model Agents with Entropic Activation Steering." ICML 2024 Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability.

comment.value:
> **Diversity of results: When I look at figures 3, 4, and 5, I feel like I'm essentially looking at different views of the same data, which makes the paper feel a bit thin from a results perspective. I think the paper would be strengthened by another set of experiments: e.g. understanding how some parameters of the task affect the downstream relationship between steering and ICL, or perhaps looking into the effects of finetuning models in the same setting – I'd be very curious to understand how it would differ from steering or ICL in changing models' behavior.**

Fair point and this was a difficulty we faced defining figures for the paper as well. Specifically, we agree that Figures 3,4,5 indeed show different views of (nearly) the same data. However, we eventually decided to show these views since they show meaningfully different information that corresponds to our three key predictions. That is, while the results are inter-related, each of these results is significant in isolation and cannot be clearly discerned from either of the other two figures.

Having said the above, we note that to enrich the diversity of results in this work, we have now included an additional Appendix D that includes results for a new set of experiments where we constructed steering vectors from ICL data. Herein, we varied the number of ICL examples used to construct steering vectors. We found that with a large enough number of ICL examples, ICL steering vectors had similar belief dynamics, although surprisingly the steering vector becomes increasingly dissimilar to the non-ICL (“0-shot”) steering vectors.

We considered adding additional experiments for other methods of altering model beliefs, such as fine-tuning and other post-training methods which update model weights, although we determined this to be outside the scope of our present work. Our belief dynamics model does not make predictions about how behavior should change as a function of the number of fine-tuning examples, or the number of epochs during training, and would require significant changes to account for these effects. One complexity of integrating this is accounting for the formation of new concepts - we explain ICL and activation steering as assigning belief over a fixed hypothesis space of concepts, but it is unclear how our model should account for the formation of and changes to the hypothesis space itself.

---

**Questions**

> **It looks like the great majority of tasks studied saturate quite quickly in n_icl_shots, c.f. the plots in figure 5 are very red. Do the authors know of tasks where this doesn't happen? Would we expect the results to be different?**

Indeed! For the tasks in our main experiments, belief saturates relatively quickly as a function of the log number of shots. The experiments we have added to Appendix F with flipped-label sentiment analysis is one example of a harder task which involves three labels, and learning a rotated mapping across these three labels. In this experiment, behavior saturates more slowly and requires more ICL examples to saturate, and does not fully plateau even with >300 in-context examples. Here we find comparable belief dynamics results as in our main experiments, where both ICL and activation steering influence belief, and our Bayesian model is very predictive of LLM behavior here as well.

----

> **How was the dataset constructed for CAA?**

For CAA, following prior work [1] we used the same dataset as was used in ICL, with 1000 positive example question-answer pairs which balance yes/no responses (i.e. 500 yes, 500 no), and 1000 negative examples which use the same questions as the positive example set but flip the yes/no answers.

[1] Panickssery, N., Gabrieli, N., Schulz, J., Tong, M., Hubinger, E., & Turner, A. (2024). Steering llama 2 via contrastive activation addition

summary.value:
The paper provides a hypothesis for ICL and activation steering: they both manipulate the internal feature representations.
With assumptions, the paper derives a formulation for the relationship between such representation change and concept probability.
Based on the derivation, the paper makes three predictions: (1) sigmoid change of concept during ICL; (2) steering will have a linear effect on log-prior odds for concept ; (3) log posterior odds will be additively impacted by varying in-context examples and steering magnitude.
The paper couples the prediction with experiments.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a unified Bayesian framework that connects in-context learning and activation steering in large language models. The authors argue that both methods operate by updating an LLM’s beliefs about latent concepts: ICL provides evidence through context, adjusting likelihoods of concepts. Activation steering modifies priors over these concepts by manipulating hidden representations.

They formalize this connection through a Belief Update Model, predicting three key phenomena: Sigmoidal learning curves for ICL as evidence accumulates. Shifts in these curves due to activation steering. Additive effects between context-based and activation-based interventions.

Empirical experiments on five “persona” datasets (e.g., Machiavellianism, Psychopathy, Narcissism, Moral Nihilism) confirm these predictions. The results show that steering magnitude and context length jointly shape model behavior, revealing phase boundaries in LLM belief states.

strengths.value:
- The used method is interesting in that it links two major inference-time control methods, prompting and activation steering under a single Bayesian belief-update paradigm.

- The Bayesian framing builds upon prior cognitive and interpretability theories, offering a formal probabilistic model of LLM behavior.

- Empirical Validation: Robust experiments across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) support the theory’s predictive accuracy.

weaknesses.value:
- The model assumes linear representation of belief and separable concept directions, which may not hold for complex or abstract concepts.

- The experiments focus on binary, persona-style datasets. Generalization to open-ended or multi-concept tasks remains uncertain.

- While the Bayesian model predicts empirical data well, it is unclear how it performs out-of-domain or on unseen LLM architectures.

comment.value:
> **To what extent do steering effects persist across layers?do certain layers dominate belief updates?**

Similar to [1], we find that the steering effect is relatively localized to a specific set of layers, with the effect peaking on a specific layer for each model (e.g. layer 12 for Llama-3.1-8b). We also find that for a given model, the same layer is optimal for all concepts that we tested. We provide further details of this layer-by-layer analysis in Appendix H. Following the Linear Representation Hypothesis, we expect that belief is linearly represented in specific layers of an LLM, where preceding layers act as an encoder and subsequent layers as a decoder from these linear beliefs. This presents a number of compelling questions for future work to explore which dive further into why this occurs, as well as the role of earlier and later layers in representing beliefs and mapping between beliefs and behaviors.

[1] Panickssery, N., Gabrieli, N., Schulz, J., Tong, M., Hubinger, E., & Turner, A. (2024). Steering llama 2 via contrastive activation addition
